title: Reformed Epistemology / Properly Basic Belief
description: A structured branching graph of Alvin Plantinga's Reformed Epistemology, exploring properly basic beliefs, the Sensus Divinitatis, Great Pumpkin objections, cognitive design plans, noetic effects of sin, and self-referential evidentialism critiques.

nodes.title: Reformed Epistemology & Properly Basic Belief (Stage 1)
nodes.summary: Formulated by Alvin Plantinga and Nicholas Wolterstorff, this view rejects Classical Evidentialism (the claim that belief in God is rational only if backed by propositional evidence). Instead, belief in God can be 'properly basic'—just like belief in memory, the external world, or other minds—arising naturally when cognitive faculties operate according to a design plan in an appropriate environment (via an innate 'Sensus Divinitatis').
nodes.summary_5th_grader: You don't need a math equation or science experiment to know your mom loves you or that yesterday really happened—you just know it instantly in your heart and mind! Alvin Plantinga argued that believing in God works the same way: God put a built-in 'God-sensor' (Sensus Divinitatis) inside us so we can know Him directly without needing a 100-page philosophical argument.

nodes.title: Deduction of Divine Cognitive Design (Stage 2)
nodes.summary: If belief in God arises as a properly basic intuition produced by cognitive faculties functioning correctly in a environment intended for human-divine communion, it implies humans were intentionally designed with a cognitive capacity (Sensus Divinitatis) specifically aimed at knowing God.
nodes.summary_5th_grader: If our built-in 'God-sensor' naturally gives us feelings of God's presence when looking at a starlit sky or praying, it means a loving God specially designed our brains to connect with Him.

nodes.title: The 'Great Pumpkin' / Anything-Goes Objection
nodes.summary: Skeptics argue that if belief in God can be basic without propositional evidence, then ANY absurd belief (e.g., belief in the Great Pumpkin returning every Halloween, or invisible teapots) could be declared 'properly basic', opening the floodgates to irrationality.
nodes.summary_5th_grader: Skeptics say: if you can just say 'I believe in God without proof because it feels right to me,' then someone else can say 'I believe a magic giant pumpkin visits every Halloween without proof!' It lets anyone believe anything crazy.

nodes.title: Basic Beliefs are Grounded, Not Arbitrary
nodes.summary: Defenders respond that 'properly basic' does not mean 'ungrounded'. Basic beliefs must be generated by cognitive faculties operating in an appropriate environment according to a design plan successfully aimed at truth. The Great Pumpkin belief lacks appropriate cognitive grounding and experiential triggers.
nodes.summary_5th_grader: Defenders reply: basic beliefs aren't just random guesses! Seeing a sunrise naturally triggers your brain to recognize God. Making up a Great Pumpkin has no built-in brain trigger—it's just a silly story, not a natural perception.

nodes.title: Subjective Groundedness vs. Public Verification
nodes.summary: Opponents reply that because internal 'groundedness' is entirely subjective, any cult leader or illusioned individual can claim their bizarre beliefs are generated by a 'properly functioning' cognitive faculty, rendering the criteria unfalsifiable.
nodes.summary_5th_grader: Skeptics push back: but since nobody else can see inside your brain, anyone in a weird cult can claim their brain has a special sensor too! You can't test or prove whose brain sensor is real.

nodes.title: Epistemic Parity with Memory and External World
nodes.summary: Plantinga demonstrates epistemic parity: you cannot publicly prove to a skeptic that other people have real minds (or that the world wasn't created 5 seconds ago with fake memories). Yet we all accept memory and other minds as basic. Demanding higher verification for God than for memory is arbitrary discrimination.
nodes.summary_5th_grader: Defenders close: you can't scientifically prove that other people have real feelings inside their heads either, or that the universe wasn't created 5 minutes ago with fake memories! Yet you trust your memory anyway. Demanding scientific proof for God while trusting your memory without proof is a double standard.

nodes.title: Evidentialist Critique (Clifford's Principle)
nodes.summary: Evidentialist philosophers (e.g., W.K. Clifford) insist that 'it is wrong always, everywhere, and for anyone, to believe anything upon insufficient evidence.' Because God's existence is not empirical, basic belief is intellectually irresponsible.
nodes.summary_5th_grader: Skeptics argue: W.K. Clifford famously said it is ALWAYS wrong and lazy to believe anything unless you have hard scientific evidence sitting right in front of you.

nodes.title: Evidentialism is Self-Referentially Incoherent
nodes.summary: Defenders point out that Clifford's rule ('believe nothing without evidence') has NO empirical evidence supporting itself! Thus, Classical Evidentialism defeats itself: if you apply Clifford's rule to Clifford's rule, you must reject Clifford's rule.
nodes.summary_5th_grader: Defenders reply: Clifford's rule destroys itself! There is zero scientific evidence proving that Clifford's rule is true. If you follow Clifford's rule, you aren't allowed to believe Clifford's rule!

nodes.title: Religious Diversity & Mutually Exclusive Intuitions
nodes.summary: Skeptics argue that different religions produce mutually exclusive 'basic' intuitions (e.g., Monotheism, Advaita Vedanta, Theravada Non-theism). If cognitive faculties reliably produce basic truth, they should not yield contradictory divine realities across cultures.
nodes.summary_5th_grader: Skeptics argue: if God built a 'God-sensor' inside human brains, why do people in different countries have completely different feelings—some feeling One God, others feeling many gods, and others feeling no god at all?

nodes.title: The Noetic Effects of Sin & Cognitive Damage
nodes.summary: Reformed thinkers reply using Calvin's concept of the 'noetic effects of sin': human rebellion and self-centeredness damage and dull the Sensus Divinitatis, distorting spiritual perception much like eye disease distorts physical vision.
nodes.summary_5th_grader: Defenders reply: just like wearing dirty sunglasses makes everything look dark, human pride and selfishness act like dirt on our spiritual eyes, blurring and distorting our built-in God-sensor!

nodes.title: The 'Sin' Explanation as Unfalsifiable Immunization
nodes.summary: Skeptics contend that claiming 'anyone who disagrees with my religion has a damaged brain sensor due to sin' is a classic unfalsifiable immunization strategy designed to dismiss opposition without argument.
nodes.summary_5th_grader: Skeptics push back: saying 'anyone who disagrees with me has a broken brain because of sin' is just a cheap trick to ignore critics without actually answering them!

nodes.title: Prevalence of Cognitive Biases Across Human Perception
nodes.summary: Defenders note that cognitive faculties are universally subject to noise, environmental damage, and psychological biases in secular domains (e.g., optical illusions, confirmation bias, moral blindness) without invalidating the baseline validity of human perception.
nodes.summary_5th_grader: Defenders conclude: optical illusions prove our eyes mess up sometimes, but that doesn't mean your eyes are totally fake! Recognizing that human brains get biased or damaged is just honest psychology.

nodes.title: Freudian Wish-Fulfillment & Psychological Illusion
nodes.summary: Freud and Feuerbach argued that belief in God is a psychological projection—an unconscious wish-fulfillment mechanism created by human vulnerability to invent a protective father figure against cosmic terror.
nodes.summary_5th_grader: Skeptics argue: Sigmund Freud said people only believe in God because life is scary, so their brains invent a super-strong sky dad to make them feel safe.

nodes.title: Genetic Fallacy & Reverse Wish-Fulfillment
nodes.summary: Defenders reply that explaining how a belief originates psychologically does not address whether the belief is true (the Genetic Fallacy). Furthermore, atheism can equally be accused of wish-fulfillment (a desire to escape divine moral accountability).
nodes.summary_5th_grader: Defenders reply: even if you wish something were true, it can still BE true! Plus, skeptics might also wish God DOESN'T exist so nobody tells them how to live their lives.

nodes.title: Plantinga's Evolutionary Argument Against Naturalism (EAAN)
nodes.summary: Plantinga flips the script with his Evolutionary Argument Against Naturalism (EAAN): if naturalism and unguided evolution are true, human cognitive faculties evolved for adaptive behavior/survival, NOT for discovering truth. This creates a defeater for trusting ANY naturalistic belief—including naturalism itself.
nodes.summary_5th_grader: Plantinga turns the tables: if evolution was just survival of the fittest without God, your brain evolved to dodge tigers, NOT to figure out cosmic truth! If naturalism is true, you can't even trust your own brain to know if naturalism is true!
